title: 2  Relations
text:
A relation records which ordered pairs from two sets are related.

Definition 2.1 (Relation) Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be sets. A relation over \(X \times Y\) is a subset \(R \subseteq X \times Y\).
If \(Y=X\), the relation is called homogeneous. When \((x,y)\in R\), we say that \(x\) is related to \(y\) and write \(xRy\).

The definition in Definition 2.1 treats a relation as a set of ordered pairs. Equivalently, its indicator is a proposition-valued function of two arguments.

Example 2.1 (Basic relations) Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be sets. The following are standard examples:

The discrete relation \(X\times Y\).
The empty relation \(\emptyset\subseteq X\times Y\).
When \(Y=X\), the diagonal relation \(\{(x,x):x\in X\}\).



Exercise 2.1 (Equality of the basic relations) Give a necessary and sufficient condition for the empty, discrete, and diagonal relations to be equal.






TipSolution





Assume the three are homogeneous relations on the same set \(X\), so \(Y=X\). They are equal if and only if \(X=\emptyset\).
If \(X=\emptyset\), then
\[
X\times X=\emptyset
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\{(x,x):x\in X\}=\emptyset,
\]
so all three relations coincide. Conversely, if the diagonal relation is empty, then \(X\) has no elements: any \(x\in X\) would make \((x,x)\) an element of the diagonal. Therefore \(X=\emptyset\).





Exercise 2.2 (Product of relations) Let \((X_1,R_1)\) and \((X_2,R_2)\) be pairs of sets and relations on them. The rule
\[
(x,y)\,(R_1\times R_2)\,(x',y')
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
xR_1x'\text{ and }yR_2y'
\]
defines a relation \(R_1\times R_2\) on \(X_1\times X_2\). Express this relation as a subset of \((X_1\times X_2)^2\).






TipSolution





The relation is
\[
R_1\times R_2
=
\left\{
\bigl((x,y),(x',y')\bigr)\in(X_1\times X_2)^2
:
(x,x')\in R_1\text{ and }(y,y')\in R_2
\right\}.
\]

title: 3  Set Identities
text:
This exercise is adapted from Abbott (2015).

Exercise 3.1 (De Morgan’s law for unions) For a sequence of sets \((A_i)_{i=1}^{\infty}\), show that
\[
\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i\right)^c
=
\bigcap_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i^c.
\]






TipSolution





We show equality by a chain of biconditionals. For arbitrary \(x\),
\[\begin{align*}
x \in \left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i\right)^c
&\iff x \notin \bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i \\
&\iff x \notin A_i \text{ for every } i\in\mathbb N \\
&\iff x \in A_i^c \text{ for every } i\in\mathbb N \\
&\iff x \in \bigcap_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i^c.
\end{align*}\]




This elementwise proof establishes the identity directly.




Abbott, Stephen. 2015. Understanding Analysis. 2nd ed. Springer. https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-1-4939-2712-8.

title: 4  Continuous Everywhere, Nowhere Differentiable
text:
4.1 Introduction
This chapter adapts the paper at source revision 612ce5f. It follows the paper’s historical motivation while tightening the main construction and proof.
In the nineteenth century, continuity was often associated with geometric smoothness. Karl Weierstrass overturned that intuition by constructing a function that is continuous at every real number and differentiable at none (Wikipedia contributors 2025b, 2025a).
A classical form of his function is
\[
W(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a^n\cos(\pi b^n x),
\]
where
\[
0<a<1,\qquad b>1\text{ is an odd integer},
\qquad ab>1+\frac{3\pi}{2}.
\]
The factor \(\pi\) is only a scaling convention: replacing \(x\) by \(x/\pi\) gives the version \(\sum a^n\cos(b^n x)\) used in the original paper. The series is built from smooth cosine waves whose amplitudes decay while their frequencies grow. The result converges to a continuous curve but retains oscillations at every scale (Stein and Shakarchi 2003).

title: 4  Continuous Everywhere, Nowhere Differentiable
text:
4.2 Background

Definition 4.1 (Continuity) Let \(f:S\to\mathbb R\) and let \(c\in S\). The function \(f\) is continuous at \(c\) if, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(\delta>0\) such that
\[
x\in S\text{ and }|x-c|<\delta
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
|f(x)-f(c)|<\varepsilon.
\]
This is the usual \(\varepsilon\)–\(\delta\) definition (Abbott 2015).


Definition 4.2 (Sequential continuity) Let \(f:S\to\mathbb R\) and let \(c\in S\). The function \(f\) is continuous at \(c\) if every sequence \((x_n)\) in \(S\) satisfying \(x_n\to c\) also satisfies \(f(x_n)\to f(c)\) (Anshelevich 2025).


Definition 4.3 (Differentiability) Let \(g:S\to\mathbb R\) be defined on an interval \(S\), and let \(c\in S\). The derivative of \(g\) at \(c\) is
\[
g'(c)=\lim_{x\to c}\frac{g(x)-g(c)}{x-c},
\]
provided this limit exists. In that case, \(g\) is differentiable at \(c\) (Abbott 2015).


Theorem 4.1 (Differentiability implies continuity) If \(g:S\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable at \(c\in S\), then \(g\) is continuous at \(c\).


Proof. Because the difference quotient tends to \(g'(c)\),
\[
\lim_{x\to c}\bigl(g(x)-g(c)\bigr)
=
\lim_{x\to c}
\left(\frac{g(x)-g(c)}{x-c}\right)(x-c)
=g'(c)\cdot0=0.
\]
Therefore \(\lim_{x\to c}g(x)=g(c)\) (Abbott 2015).

The converse fails even for familiar functions.

Example 4.1 (The absolute-value cusp) The function \(f(x)=|x|\) is continuous at \(0\), but
\[
\lim_{x\to0^-}\frac{|x|}{x}=-1
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\lim_{x\to0^+}\frac{|x|}{x}=1.
\]
Thus \(f'(0)\) does not exist (Abbott 2015).

This example has only one corner. Weierstrass’s construction is more striking because it has no differentiable point at all.

title: 4  Continuous Everywhere, Nowhere Differentiable
text:
4.3 Construction
We need three elementary estimates.

Lemma 4.1 (Cosine is Lipschitz) For all \(x,y\in\mathbb R\),
\[
|\cos x-\cos y|\le |x-y|.
\]


Proof. The mean value theorem gives \(\cos x-\cos y=-\sin(\xi)(x-y)\) for some \(\xi\) between \(x\) and \(y\). Since \(|\sin\xi|\le1\), the claim follows.


Lemma 4.2 (A nearby cosine oscillation) For every \(c\in\mathbb R\) and every positive integer \(k\), there exists
\[
y\in\left(c+\frac{\pi}{k},c+\frac{3\pi}{k}\right)
\]
such that
\[
|\cos(kc)-\cos(ky)|\ge1.
\]


Proof. As \(y\) traverses this interval, \(ky\) traverses an open interval of length \(2\pi\). Put \(r=\cos(kc)\). If \(-1<r<1\), the interval contains points where cosine equals both \(-1\) and \(1\), so one of those values differs from \(r\) by at least \(1\). If \(r=1\) or \(r=-1\), the interval contains a point where cosine is \(0\), again giving a difference of \(1\).


Lemma 4.3 (Integer shifts of cosine) For every integer \(r\) and every real \(t\),
\[
\cos(r\pi+t)=(-1)^r\cos t.
\]


Proof. Apply the cosine addition formula and use \(\sin(r\pi)=0\) and \(\cos(r\pi)=(-1)^r\).


Lemma 4.4 (Three-term reverse triangle inequality) For all real numbers \(u,v,w\),
\[
|u+v+w|\ge |u|-|v|-|w|.
\]


Proof. Twice applying the triangle inequality gives \(|u|\le |u+v+w|+|v|+|w|\).


Theorem 4.2 (Absolute convergence) For every \(x\in\mathbb R\), the series
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a^n\cos(\pi b^n x)
\]
converges absolutely.


Proof. Since \(|\cos(\pi b^n x)|\le1\),
\[
|a^n\cos(\pi b^n x)|\le a^n.
\]
The geometric series \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a^n\) converges because \(0<a<1\). Comparison proves absolute convergence (Massachusetts Institute of Technology 2020).

title: 4  Continuous Everywhere, Nowhere Differentiable
text:
4.4 Continuity

Theorem 4.3 (Continuity of the Weierstrass function) The function
\[
W(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a^n\cos(\pi b^n x)
\]
is bounded and continuous on \(\mathbb R\).


Proof. For every \(x\),
\[
|W(x)|
\le \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a^n
=\frac{1}{1-a},
\]
so \(W\) is bounded. The same estimate is independent of \(x\), so the Weierstrass M-test shows that the partial sums converge uniformly. Every partial sum is continuous, and a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous (Massachusetts Institute of Technology 2020).







NoteSequential proof





The original paper also proves continuity using Definition 4.2. Let \(x_j\to c\) and fix \(\varepsilon>0\). Choose \(M\) so large that
\[
2\sum_{n=M+1}^{\infty}a^n<\frac{\varepsilon}{2}.
\]
We split the series into a finite head and a uniformly small tail. For the head, continuity of each cosine term gives
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{M}a^n
\left|\cos(\pi b^n x_j)-\cos(\pi b^n c)\right|
\longrightarrow0.
\]
It is therefore less than \(\varepsilon/2\) for all sufficiently large \(j\). The tail satisfies
\[
\sum_{n=M+1}^{\infty}a^n
\left|\cos(\pi b^n x_j)-\cos(\pi b^n c)\right|
\le2\sum_{n=M+1}^{\infty}a^n
<\frac{\varepsilon}{2}.
\]
Hence \(|W(x_j)-W(c)|<\varepsilon\) eventually, so \(W(x_j)\to W(c)\) (Massachusetts Institute of Technology 2020).



The original paper approached continuity sequentially and used the following useful fact.

Exercise 4.1 (A limsup criterion for convergence to zero) Prove that
\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}|x_n|=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\lim_{n\to\infty}x_n=0.
\]






TipSolution





If \(x_n\to0\), then \(|x_n|\to0\), so \(\limsup |x_n|=0\).
Conversely, suppose \(\limsup |x_n|=0\). Because \(|x_n|\ge0\), we also have \(\liminf |x_n|\ge0\). Hence
\[
0\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}|x_n|
\le\limsup_{n\to\infty}|x_n|=0.
\]
Thus \(|x_n|\to0\), which is equivalent to \(x_n\to0\).

title: 4  Continuous Everywhere, Nowhere Differentiable
text:
4.5 Nowhere differentiability

Theorem 4.4 (Weierstrass) Assume
\[
0<a<1,
\qquad b>1\text{ is an odd integer},
\qquad ab>1+\frac{3\pi}{2}.
\]
Then
\[
W(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a^n\cos(\pi b^n x)
\]
is nowhere differentiable on \(\mathbb R\).


Proof. Fix \(x_0\in\mathbb R\). For each \(m\), choose an integer \(k_m\) nearest to \(b^m x_0\) and write
\[
z_m=b^m x_0-k_m,
\qquad -\frac12\le z_m\le\frac12.
\]
Set
\[
x_m=\frac{k_m+1}{b^m},
\qquad
h_m=x_m-x_0=\frac{1-z_m}{b^m}.
\]
Then
\[
\frac{1}{2b^m}\le h_m\le\frac{3}{2b^m},
\]
so \(x_m\to x_0\) from the right. Split the increment as
\[
W(x_m)-W(x_0)=A_m+B_m,
\]
where \(A_m\) contains the terms \(0\le n<m\) and \(B_m\) contains the terms \(n\ge m\).
By Lemma 4.1,
\[
\begin{aligned}
|A_m|
&\le \pi h_m\sum_{n=0}^{m-1}(ab)^n \\
&\le \frac{\pi(ab)^m}{ab-1}h_m.
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(n\ge m\), the oddness of \(b\) and Lemma 4.3 give
\[
\cos(\pi b^n x_m)=-(-1)^{k_m}
\]
and
\[
\cos(\pi b^n x_0)
=(-1)^{k_m}\cos(\pi b^{n-m}z_m).
\]
Therefore
\[
B_m=-(-1)^{k_m}
\sum_{n=m}^{\infty}a^n
\left(1+\cos(\pi b^{n-m}z_m)\right).
\]
Every summand in parentheses is nonnegative. Keeping only the \(n=m\) term and using \(|z_m|\le1/2\) yields
\[
|B_m|
\ge a^m\bigl(1+\cos(\pi z_m)\bigr)
\ge a^m.
\]
Since \(h_m\le 3/(2b^m)\),
\[
|B_m|\ge\frac23(ab)^m h_m.
\]
The reverse triangle inequality now gives
\[
\left|\frac{W(x_m)-W(x_0)}{x_m-x_0}\right|
\ge
(ab)^m\left(\frac23-\frac{\pi}{ab-1}\right).
\]
The parenthesized constant is positive precisely when \(ab>1+3\pi/2\), and \((ab)^m\to\infty\). Thus the difference quotients along \(x_m\to x_0\) are unbounded, so \(W'(x_0)\) does not exist. Because \(x_0\) was arbitrary, \(W\) is nowhere differentiable (Massachusetts Institute of Technology 2020).

title: 4  Continuous Everywhere, Nowhere Differentiable
text:
4.6 Conclusion
The Weierstrass function separates continuity from smoothness in the strongest possible way. Its partial sums are smooth, and they converge uniformly, yet the limiting curve remains jagged at every scale. The example shows both the reach and the limits of geometric intuition: continuity survives uniform limits, while differentiability need not.




Abbott, Stephen. 2015. Understanding Analysis. 2nd ed. Springer. https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-1-4939-2712-8.


Anshelevich, Michael. 2025. Class Notes for MATH 409.


Massachusetts Institute of Technology. 2020. Real Analysis Lecture 18: Weierstrass’s Example of a Continuous and Nowhere Differentiable Function. https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-100a-real-analysis-fall-2020/mit18_100af20_lec18.pdf.


Stein, Elias M., and Rami Shakarchi. 2003. Fourier Analysis: An Introduction. Vol. 1. Princeton Lectures in Analysis. Princeton University Press. https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691113845/fourier-analysis.

title: 5  Vector Spaces
text:
This exercise is adapted from Axler (2024).

Exercise 5.1 (Double additive inverse) Prove that \(-(-v)=v\) for every \(v\in V\).






TipSolution





Let \(v\in V\). By definition, \(-v\) is an additive inverse of \(v\), so
\[
v+(-v)=0.
\]
Commutativity gives \((-v)+v=0\). But \(-(-v)\) is also defined by
\[
(-v)+(-(-v))=0.
\]
Because additive inverses are unique, \(-(-v)=v\).




The statement only uses the additive-group structure; no scalar multiplication is needed.




Axler, Sheldon. 2024. Linear Algebra Done Right. 4th ed. Undergraduate Texts in Mathematics. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-41026-0.

title: 6  Convex Sets
text:
These exercises are adapted from Boyd and Vandenberghe (2004).

Exercise 6.1 (Finite convex combinations) Let \(C \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) be a convex set, with \(x_1, \ldots, x_k \in C\), and let \(\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_k \in \mathbb{R}\) satisfy
\[
\theta_i \geq 0,
\qquad
\theta_1 + \cdots + \theta_k = 1.
\]
Show that
\[
\theta_1x_1 + \cdots + \theta_kx_k \in C.
\]
The definition of convexity gives this result for \(k=2\); prove it for arbitrary \(k\).
Hint. Use induction on \(k\).






TipSolution





We prove the result by induction on the number of points.
The case \(k=1\) is immediate: the coefficient condition forces \(\theta_1=1\), so \(\theta_1x_1=x_1\in C\).
For the first nontrivial case, let \(k=2\). If \(x_1,x_2\in C\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\), then the definition of convexity gives
\[
(1-\theta)x_1+\theta x_2\in C.
\]
Thus every convex combination of two points in \(C\) belongs to \(C\).
Now suppose every convex combination of \(\ell\) points in \(C\) belongs to \(C\). In other words, whenever
\[
x_i\in C,
\qquad
\theta_i\geq0,
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\theta_i=1,
\]
we have
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\theta_i x_i\in C.
\]
Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_{\ell+1}\in C\), and let \(\phi_i\geq0\) satisfy
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell+1}\phi_i=1.
\]
If \(\phi_{\ell+1}=1\), then \(\phi_1=\cdots=\phi_\ell=0\), so
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell+1}\phi_i x_i=x_{\ell+1}\in C.
\]
Now suppose \(\phi_{\ell+1}<1\), and define
\[
z=\frac{1}{1-\phi_{\ell+1}}
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\phi_i x_i.
\]
Since
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\phi_i=1-\phi_{\ell+1},
\]
the coefficients in the definition of \(z\) are nonnegative and sum to one. The induction hypothesis therefore implies that \(z\in C\).
Finally,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell+1}\phi_i x_i
&=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\phi_i x_i+\phi_{\ell+1}x_{\ell+1} \\
&=(1-\phi_{\ell+1})z+\phi_{\ell+1}x_{\ell+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Because \(z,x_{\ell+1}\in C\) and \(\phi_{\ell+1}\in[0,1]\), convexity of \(C\) gives
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell+1}\phi_i x_i\in C.
\]
Therefore, by induction, every finite convex combination of points in \(C\) belongs to \(C\).





Exercise 6.2 (Distance between parallel hyperplanes) For \(a\neq0\), what is the distance between the parallel hyperplanes
\[
H_1=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid a^Tx=b_1\}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
H_2=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid a^Tx=b_2\}?
\]






TipSolution





For every \(x_1\in H_1\) and \(x_2\in H_2\),
\[
a^T(x_1-x_2)=b_1-b_2.
\]
The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality therefore gives
\[
|b_1-b_2|
=|a^T(x_1-x_2)|
\leq\lVert a\rVert\,\lVert x_1-x_2\rVert.
\]
Thus every pair of points, one from each hyperplane, satisfies
\[
\lVert x_1-x_2\rVert
\geq
\frac{|b_1-b_2|}{\lVert a\rVert}.
\]
This lower bound is attained. Choose any \(x_2\in H_2\) and define
\[
x_1=x_2+\frac{b_1-b_2}{\lVert a\rVert^2}a.
\]
Then
\[
a^Tx_1
=a^Tx_2+\frac{b_1-b_2}{\lVert a\rVert^2}a^Ta
=b_2+(b_1-b_2)
=b_1,
\]
so \(x_1\in H_1\), and
\[
\lVert x_1-x_2\rVert
=\left\lVert\frac{b_1-b_2}{\lVert a\rVert^2}a\right\rVert
=\frac{|b_1-b_2|}{\lVert a\rVert}.
\]
Hence the distance between the hyperplanes is
\[
\boxed{\frac{|b_1-b_2|}{\lVert a\rVert}}.
\]





Exercise 6.3 (Voronoi description of a halfspace) Let \(a\) and \(b\) be distinct points in \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Show that the set of all points that are closer in Euclidean norm to \(a\) than to \(b\),
\[
\{x\mid \lVert x-a\rVert_2\leq\lVert x-b\rVert_2\},
\]
is a halfspace. Describe it explicitly as an inequality of the form \(c^Tx\leq d\). Draw a picture.






TipSolution





Since both sides are nonnegative,
\[
\lVert x-a\rVert_2\leq\lVert x-b\rVert_2
\iff
\lVert x-a\rVert_2^2\leq\lVert x-b\rVert_2^2.
\]
Expanding the squared norms gives
\[
\lVert x-a\rVert_2^2=x^Tx-2a^Tx+a^Ta,
\qquad
\lVert x-b\rVert_2^2=x^Tx-2b^Tx+b^Tb.
\]
The quadratic terms cancel, leaving
\[
2(b-a)^Tx\leq b^Tb-a^Ta.
\]
Thus
\[
\{x\mid\lVert x-a\rVert_2\leq\lVert x-b\rVert_2\}
=
\{x\mid c^Tx\leq d\},
\]
where
\[
c=b-a,
\qquad
d=\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\lVert b\rVert_2^2-\lVert a\rVert_2^2\bigr).
\]
Since \(a\neq b\), we have \(c\neq0\), so this is a halfspace. Geometrically, its boundary is the perpendicular bisector of the segment \([a,b]\), and the halfspace contains \(a\).








Boyd, Stephen, and Lieven Vandenberghe. 2004. Convex Optimization. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511804441.
